new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File opened: (symlink to; 60pp, ANU Open Research CC BY-SA edition of PL C-54:653-712). PDF page 7 = printed p.659, rendered at 150 dpi and read as an image. Under '3. GRAMMAR / 3.1. Consonants, Vowels and Stress' (the section opens on p.658 with 'the phonemic inventory of the W. By. languages..', i.e. it is written for the whole West Barkly group), after the note that gy 'also occurs in Ng. (extensively)', the page reads exactly: 'Stress normally falls on the penultimate syllable of the word-unit. There are few exceptions. With the addition of suffixes to a stem, stress moves to the penultimate vowel of the series of suffixes, e.g.: Dj. ṇayúlu two women (nom) / ṇayuilíŋa two women (erg) /…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the (suffixed) word; when suffixes are added stress shifts rightward so that it stays penultimate. Chadwick states this once for all five West Barkly lects including Ngarnga/Ngarndji (for which he was the 1960s-70s fieldworker); the illustrating forms are Djingili.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the 'word-unit' (stem plus suffixes); stress recomputed after suffixation. CAVEATS: (i) the statement is family-wide, not Ngarnka-specific, and no Ngarnka forms are stress-marked; (ii) Nordlinger 1998:33 fn.23 explicitly rejects Chadwick's (1978:17) blanket penultimate claim for closely related Wambaya, which she shows has initial/morpheme-initial stress, so the claim's validity for Ngarnka (Wambaya's closest relative in the Ngurlun branch) is uncertain; (iii) Goedemans 1998 App. D p.245 independently files 'Ngarndji' under penultimate stress citing Chadwick 1971 (the Ngarndji-specific wordlist and phonological key), which we could not open.
new_statements.identity_note: Chadwick 1979 uses 'Ngarnga, Ngarndji (Ng.)' for Glottolog ngar1283 Ngarnka; his stress sentence is stated once for the whole West Barkly group (Djingili djin1251, Ngarnga ngar1283, and the McArthur lects Wambaya/Gudanji/Binbinka wamb1258), with Djingili examples, so it is first-hand but not Ngarnka-specific. Note ISO 639-3 nji ('Gudanji') conflates Ngarnka with Gudanji, which Glottolog treats as a Wambaya dialect; Goedemans 1998's 'Ngarndji' entry and Chadwick 1971 refer to Ngarnka proper (ngar1283). Nordlinger 1998 disputes Chadwick's penultimate claim for Wambaya (initial stress), so the Ngarnka reading should be flagged as contested/low-confidence until Chadwick 1971 or Osgarby 2014 is seen.

sources.citation: Nordlinger, Rachel. 1998. A grammar of Wambaya, Northern Territory (Australia). Pacific Linguistics C-140. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: p.33 fn.23 (in the Wambaya stress section): 'I disagree with Chadwick (e.g. 1978:17) who claims that primary stress in all of the West Barkly languages falls on the penultimate syllable of the word.' -- second-hand report locating Chadwick's group-wide penultimate claim at 1978:17, and showing it is wrong for closely related Wambaya (initial/morpheme-initial stress). Nothing specific on Ngarnga stress.
